topic: The Browser Wars: Edge’s Quiet Takeover

In this chart-race, we track the real pivot of the browser era—from Internet Explorer’s peak dominance to Edge’s rise alongside a Chrome powerhouse.

instagram_caption:
🚀 Internet Explorer hit ~60%—then quietly got erased. And Microsoft Edge took the crown by inches, not miracles.

Here’s the browser timeline most people forget: in 2008, Internet Explorer was the default web door for tens of millions of people. Roughly ~60% of global browser traffic ran through IE. Even as competitors existed, IE sat on top like a permanent landmark.

Then the floor started moving. By 2011, IE’s share slid to about ~45%. By 2012 it was ~37.5%, and by 2013 it dropped near ~30%. The story wasn’t just “new browsers showed up”—it was performance, standards, and user trust. Chrome went from a tiny slice (single digits) into the mainstream, while IE kept losing mindshare year after year.

Edge enters the chat. Early years were small—around ~0–1% in the early period—yet the trend is what matters. From ~5% mid-decade, Edge kept climbing as users modernized. By 2019 Edge was around ~15%, and by 2021 it reached ~20%. During 2023–2025, Edge continued its steady ascent to roughly ~24–26.5%, while Internet Explorer sank to about ~1% and then below.

Meanwhile, Chrome stayed the heavyweight: from ~4% in 2008 to the low-60s in the mid/late 2020s (about ~62% by 2026 in this chart). Firefox, once a serious contender (~20–22%), tapered down to the low single digits by the mid-2020s.

So the dramatic part isn’t just Edge winning—it’s how IE went from “the web” to a rounding error.

facebook_caption:
Internet Explorer’s decline is one of the clearest “platform collapse” stories in modern computing. In 2008, IE commanded roughly ~60% of global browser traffic. Over the next decade, its share eroded year by year—falling to ~45% by 2011, ~30% by 2013, and eventually reaching around ~1% by the early-to-mid 2020s.

At the same time, the browser landscape consolidated. Google Chrome expanded from the high-single-digit range in the late 2000s to the low-60% range by the mid/late 2020s, reflecting long-term momentum in speed, extensions, and standards adoption. Firefox rose early (about ~20–22% in the early 2010s) but gradually tapered down to the low single digits by the mid-2020s.

Microsoft Edge, meanwhile, shows a different arc: it starts near zero and grows steadily—about ~5% mid-decade, ~15% by 2019, ~20% by 2021, and roughly ~26–27% by 2025–2026. This makes the “browser wars” chart dramatic in two ways: IE collapses fast, Chrome stays powerful, and Edge climbs persistently.

threads_caption:
Remember when Internet Explorer basically WAS the internet? 😬

In 2008 it was around ~60% browser share… and then the slide happened. By the early 2010s it’s dropping fast (mid/high-30s to ~30%), while Chrome ramps up hard into the mainstream.

The twist: Edge doesn’t explode—it climbs. From near ~0–1% early on to ~15% by 2019, ~20% by 2021, and ~26–27% by 2025–2026. Meanwhile Chrome holds the heavyweight role (low-60s), and Firefox fades from ~20%+ down to a few percent.

If this timeline were a real-life race, IE is the car that breaks down early—Edge is the steady driver who keeps gaining lanes.
